claims.text: The reported HfNbTiVAl10 alloy has a hierarchical heterostructure with multilevel chemical fluctuations.
High-throughput nanoindentation and micro-tensile testing synchronized with DIC can capture spatiotemporal local strain data during tensile and fracture experiments.
The synchronized testing and DIC setup can capture micro-crack initiation events.
A machine-learning model trained on these experimental data can predict macroscopic Young's modulus, yield strength, and fracture toughness.
Local strain fluctuations and micro-crack initiation mediate the relationship between microstructural heterogeneity and macroscopic mechanical properties.
Dense spatiotemporal data permit machine learning to learn a mapping from local deformation features to bulk mechanical responses.
Local stress-concentration and crack-onset indicators improve the prediction of fracture toughness.
The experimental machine-learning approach can bypass computationally expensive simulations.
The proposed method will reduce prediction time from hours to minutes.
The proposed method will improve predictive accuracy by roughly 20% relative to current simulation-based methods.
The expected accuracy improvement is particularly applicable to fracture-toughness prediction.
First-principles, CALPHAD, and mesoscale simulation approaches have high computational demands.
Existing simulation and static-data approaches are less reliable for predicting fracture behavior.
The method may become unreliable when DIC lacks sufficient resolution to resolve rapid or highly localized deformation.
The method may become unreliable under extreme strain rates or non-ambient conditions.
Prediction performance depends on dataset quality and DIC spatial and temporal resolution.
Experimental noise and inadequate sampling of rare microstructural events can impair model performance.
